questions.q: A 1D signal of length $n = 32$ goes through a kernel of size $k = 5$ with padding $p = 2$ and stride $s = 2$. How long is the output, using $\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1$?
questions.explain: $\lfloor (32 + 4 - 5)/2 \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor 31/2 \rfloor + 1 = 15 + 1 = 16$. The trap is forgetting the $+1$ (15), or assuming padding 2 keeps the size 32 — it only does so when the stride is 1.

questions.q: What do deep-learning libraries actually compute in a "convolution" layer?
options: True convolution: the kernel is flipped before sliding
Cross-correlation: the kernel slides over the input without flipping
An element-wise product of the whole input with the kernel, with no sliding
A Fourier transform of the input
questions.explain: Frameworks slide the kernel unflipped (cross-correlation). Because the kernel is learned, the network simply learns the flipped weights, so the naming difference doesn't matter in practice — but it does when you copy a textbook kernel like Sobel.

questions.q: A conv layer has $3\times3$ kernels, 3 input channels and 16 output channels (with one bias per output channel). How many parameters does it have on a $224\times224$ image?
questions.explain: Parameter sharing: the same $k^2 C_{in} C_{out}$ weights plus $C_{out}$ biases are reused at every position, so the count ($448$) does not depend on the image size at all.

questions.q: You stack three $3\times3$ conv layers with stride 1. How wide is the receptive field of one output unit along each axis?
questions.explain: With stride 1 each layer adds $k - 1 = 2$: $1 + 3\cdot 2 = 7$. It grows linearly, not multiplicatively — that only happens when strides (or pooling) make the jump grow.
